own_scenes.desc: Cada avance llegó con palizas y asesinatos televisados: Little Rock, los Freedom Riders, Birmingham, los tres activistas muertos en el Freedom Summer de 1964. El «Bloody Sunday» del puente Edmund Pettus en Selma (marzo de 1965) empujó a Johnson a la Ley de Derecho al Voto, firmada el 6 de agosto; Malcolm X había sido asesinado en febrero. Cinco días después ardía Watts: seis días de disturbios, treinta y cuatro muertos, la rebelión de un gueto zonificado para la pobreza. La no violencia de Martin Luther King se resquebrajaba y el SNCC, más joven y radical, se alejaba de la SCLC. Muy pocos discos negros hablaban de los derechos civiles («A Change Is Gonna Come» de Sam Cooke, «Keep on Pushing» y «People Get Ready» de los Impressions; «Mississippi Goddam» de Nina Simone fue prohibido), pero el público oía mensajes en «Dancing in the Street», «Shotgun» o «Nowhere to Run», metáforas de lo que aún no se podía decir. El 5 de junio de 1966 James Meredith empezó su Marcha contra el Miedo de Memphis a Jackson; al segundo día le dispararon y los líderes de todos los grupos la continuaron juntos por última vez.

refs.q: The events in Selma made national news and quickly gained their own term – ‘Bloody Sunday’.
refs.para: The flickering television images still make the blood boil. But, in early March 1965, they were even more shocking. The events in Selma made national news and quickly gained their own term – ‘Bloody Sunday’. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee’s leader, John Lewis, at the very front of the march, was hospitalised with a fractured skull, while fifty-four-year-old Amelia Boynton, a long-standing and well-respected civil rights activist, was gassed and beaten unconscious.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.para: Watts was a war zone. Dramatic pictures of fire billowing above the Los Angeles streets shocked a nation, but the riots didn’t stop. After two days of intensifying disturbances, the National Guard was called in. It took another three days for an uneasy calm to settle over the ravaged district, by which time an estimated $40 million worth of damage had been caused and thirty-four black citizens killed.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: The simple fact was that, in all this turmoil, black R&B and pop had struggled to make overt statements.
refs.para: The simple fact was that, in all this turmoil, black R&B and pop had struggled to make overt statements. The music and the movement were inextricable, but it’s startling just how few mid-sixties black American R&B and pop records directly addressed civil rights: the most obvious were Sam Cooke’s hymnal ‘A Change Is Gonna Come’, a Top 40 hit in early 1965 before its revival later that year by Otis Redding; and the Impressions’ 1964 ‘Keep on Pushing’ and ‘People Get Ready’.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: Three days later, James Meredith began his ‘March Against Fear’.
refs.para: Three days later, James Meredith began his ‘March Against Fear’. A USAAF veteran, Meredith had been national news in 1962, when he became the first black American student to be admitted into the segregated University of Mississippi. After weeks of rebuffs and legal arguments, Meredith actually entered the campus on 1 October, triggering a riot that involved US marshals, snipers and US Army troops. Two people died and over two hundred were injured.
